chief_complaint: racing heart, dizziness when standing up, and extreme brain fog for 8 months
hpi_details: 8-month history of debilitating lightheadedness, rapid pounding heart rate, and near-syncope that occurs almost exclusively upon standing or sitting upright from a recumbent position. Symptoms improve significantly within minutes of lying down. Accompanied by chronic severe fatigue, poor concentration ('brain fog'), and purple discoloration of her lower legs when standing (acrocyanosis). Symptoms began 4 weeks after a documented bout of infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever). Denies true loss of consciousness.
ideas: thinks her nervous system has lost the ability to control her blood vessels since getting glandular fever
concerns: frustrated because previous doctors dismissed her symptoms as anxiety or physical deconditioning
expectations: wants a tilt-table test or specialized autonomic testing and practical medication to lower her standing pulse
pmh: infectious mononucleosis 9 months ago, joint hypermobility syndrome (Ehlers-Danlos hypermobile type traits), irritable bowel syndrome
social_hx: postgraduate psychology student currently on leave of absence due to fatigue, non-smoker

clinical_knowledge.topic: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes validating the patient's symptoms as a recognized autonomic disorder and starting with non-pharmacological measures, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: racing heart, dizziness when standing up, and extreme brain fog for 8 months

Key HPI features: 8-month history of debilitating lightheadedness, rapid pounding heart rate, and near-syncope that occurs almost exclusively upon standing or sitting upright from a recumbent position. Symptoms improve significantly within minutes of lying down. Accompanied by chronic severe fatigue, poor concentration ('brain fog'), and purple discoloration of her lower legs when standing (acrocyanosis). Symptoms began 4 weeks after a documented bout of infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever). Denies true loss of consciousness.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform a 10-minute Active Stand Test (or head-up tilt-table test): measure baseline recumbent HR and BP after 5 mins supine, then check HR and BP at 1, 3, 5, and 10 minutes of active standing. Adult diagnostic criteria include a sustained heart-rate increase of >=30 bpm within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of orthostatic hypotension; an absolute HR >=120 bpm may occur but is not required. Bloods: FBC, ferritin, thyroid function, morning cortisol, autoimmune panel. Baseline ECG and 24-hour Holter monitor.
Relevant background/PMH: infectious mononucleosis 9 months ago, joint hypermobility syndrome (Ehlers-Danlos hypermobile type traits), irritable bowel syndrome
Current medications: propranolol 10mg PRN with limited benefit
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Orthostatic hypotension without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope with injury, or symptoms present while lying flat.
management_principles: Validate patient's symptoms as a recognized autonomic disorder
Non-pharmacological management first: increased oral fluid intake and sodium supplementation individualized to comorbidities and contraindications
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society Expert Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Postural Tachycardia Syndrome, Inappropriate Sinus Tachycardia, and Vasovagal Syncope

reference_soap.subjective: 25F with joint hypermobility presents with 8-month postural tachycardia, orthostatic presyncope, dependent leg acrocyanosis, and cognitive fatigue triggered post-viral infection.
reference_soap.objective: Perform a 10-minute Active Stand Test (or head-up tilt-table test): measure baseline recumbent HR and BP after 5 mins supine, then check HR and BP at 1, 3, 5, and 10 minutes of active standing. Adult diagnostic criteria include a sustained heart-rate increase of >=30 bpm within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of orthostatic hypotension; an absolute HR >=120 bpm may occur but is not required. Bloods: FBC, ferritin, thyroid function, morning cortisol, autoimmune panel. Baseline ECG and 24-hour Holter monitor.
reference_soap.assessment: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) post-viral onset. DDx: orthostatic hypotension, inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST), chronic fatigue syndrome / ME, adrenal insufficiency, phaeochromocytoma, anxiety disorder.
reference_soap.plan: Validate patient's symptoms as a recognized autonomic disorder. Start non-pharmacological management with increased oral fluids and sodium individualized to comorbidities and contraindications. Compression garments (waist-high 30-40 mmHg compression stockings/abdominal binders). Structured recumbent exercise conditioning protocol (rowing, recumbent cycling, swimming) avoiding upright exertion initially. Pharmacological treatment if refractory should be individualized by a clinician; options may include low-dose beta-blocker, ivabradine, midodrine, or fludrocortisone. Cardiology/autonomic specialist referral.

learning_objectives: Apply diagnostic criteria for Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome: sustained HR rise >=30 bpm on standing without orthostatic hypotension
Recognise the clinical overlap between autonomic dysregulation, post-viral syndromes, and joint hypermobility (Ehlers-Danlos)
Formulate comprehensive non-pharmacological volume expansion strategies (3L fluid + 8-10g sodium + waist-high compression)
Validate patient experiences of autonomic chronic illness empathetically while structuring a graded recumbent rehabilitation plan

teaching.one_liner: On standing, the heart races without the blood pressure dropping — often after a viral illness, and disabling out of proportion to the findings.
red_flags: Syncope with injury, or symptoms present while lying flat

must_ask.say: Does it happen specifically when you stand up, and settle when you lie down?
How long after standing do the symptoms start?
Did this all start after an infection or a period of being unwell?
How is your energy and concentration on a normal day?
How much do you drink in a day, and do you add salt to your food?
What has this stopped you doing?

history.answer: Whenever I stand up, my heart starts racing and pounding, and I feel really dizzy and foggy-headed. It has been happening for eight months, and it's making it impossible to function.
My heart suddenly pounds very hard and fast against my ribs as soon as I'm upright. It feels like a steady racing sensation rather than skipping beats or fluttering irregularly.
It beats in a very steady, regular rhythm, like a rapid metronome. It's just beating much too fast whenever I'm on my feet.
The racing starts within a minute or two of standing up from bed or a chair. Once I lie completely flat again, it settles down within a few minutes.
It happens every single day, practically every time I get on my feet. As long as I remain standing, my heart keeps pounding and won't slow down.
It is definitely triggered by standing upright or even sitting up straight for too long. If I stay lying flat, my heart feels completely normal.
Lying down flat on my back is the only thing that brings quick relief. Drinking cold water or resting while still sitting upright doesn't help much.
I get intensely lightheaded and feel like I am about to pass out, but I've never completely lost consciousness. It happens even when I'm just standing still, not only during exercise.
I feel tight in my chest and a bit breathless because my heart is pounding so fast, but I don't have crushing chest pain. The feeling goes away when I lie down.
I feel much worse in hot weather and warm showers, but I haven't had sudden unexplained weight loss or heavy sweating. My hands don't shake either.
I have severe, exhausting fatigue every day, along with intense brain fog. I have trouble concentrating, reading, or remembering things when I'm upright.
No, my menstrual periods are completely normal and not unusually heavy. I've never noticed black tarry stools, vomiting blood, or easy bruising.
I get a dull pressure headache when I stand, but I don't get sudden severe pounding headaches with cold sweats or facial pallor. I also don't get shaky or sweaty when I skip a meal.
I don't have sudden waves of panic, a sense of doom, or hyperventilating while resting comfortably. Other doctors told me it was just anxiety, but it only happens physically when I stand up.

About nine months ago, I had a severe case of mononucleosis with fever, fatigue, and swollen neck glands. These heart-racing and dizziness spells started about four weeks after I thought I had recovered.
Yes, whenever I stand still for a few minutes, my feet and lower legs turn a mottled reddish-purple color. The color goes right back to normal when I put my legs up.
I drink about one to one and a half liters of plain water a day and eat normal meals. I haven't been adding extra salt or drinking special electrolyte solutions.
It has completely derailed my life. I had to take a leave of absence from my master's degree in psychology because I couldn't stand during classes or think clearly.

I suspect that glandular fever somehow damaged my nervous system's ability to control my blood vessels. It has been so frustrating because past doctors dismissed me as anxious or out of shape, and I really want autonomic testing to get answers.
I don't drink energy drinks, and I only drink half a cup of weak tea in the morning because caffeine makes my heart race even faster. I rarely drink alcohol, maybe one glass of wine every few months.
No, I never take over-the-counter cold medicines, decongestant nasal sprays, diet pills, or asthma inhalers.

Aside from that bout of mono, I have irritable bowel syndrome and unusually loose, flexible joints that doctors called hypermobility syndrome. I have never had high blood pressure or heart problems before this.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been hospitalized overnight.
A doctor gave me propranolol ten milligrams to take as needed, but it hasn't helped much. I am not taking any other prescription medications or herbal supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes, and I don't use recreational drugs or vape.
I live in an apartment with a roommate. I was studying for my master's in psychology, but I'm currently on medical leave.
No one in my family died suddenly at a young age or had heart arrhythmias or cardiomyopathy. My mother does have very flexible, loose joints like mine.
My last period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days. I am not currently sexually active, so there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Supine BP is 116/72 mmHg with HR 68 bpm; upon standing, BP remains stable at 114/74 mmHg while HR rises to 104 bpm at 3 minutes and 112 bpm at 10 minutes without orthostatic hypotension.
The patient is resting comfortably in the supine position, appearing mildly fatigued but in no acute cardiopulmonary distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact without lid lag or proptosis.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and smooth without palpable nodules or bruits.
No resting, postural, or kinetic tremor observed in outstretched hands.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm while supine; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or clicks.
Bilateral breath sounds are clear to auscultation without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are bilaterally symmetric, strong, and regular at 68 bpm while supine.
Demonstrates generalized joint hypermobility with bilateral thumb apposition to forearm and knee hyperextension, without joint effusion or tenderness.
Dependent reddish-purple mottled discoloration noted over bilateral lower legs and feet on prolonged standing, which rapidly resolves upon lying down; skin is soft and mildly hyperextensible.
